A1.justification: Both PDFs describe SandboxEscapeBench, and their main text, figures, tables and complete appendices are readable and matchable. The later version contains reporting inconsistencies, but these do not prevent comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluations of nine models on 18 container-escape tasks, including compute scaling, hinting experiments and transcript analyses.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds five-model evaluations, extended token budgets, expanded transcript audits and independent expert difficulty ratings.

M1.justification: The nested VM/container architecture, ReAct harness, bash and submit tools, prompts and flag-retrieval procedure remain unchanged. The explicit ReAct description in v2's main text was already documented in v1 Appendix E; evaluating newer models does not introduce a new proposed method.

E1.justification: Table 1 retains the same 18 orchestration, runtime and kernel tasks, exploit conditions and canonical difficulty ratings. Renaming scenarios to tasks, evaluating newer models and increasing token budgets do not expand task coverage.

E2.justification: Figure 2 expands the evaluated comparison from nine to fourteen models by adding Claude Mythos Preview, Claude Opus 4.6 and 4.7, GPT-5.4 Pro and GPT-5.5. These models also appear in the expanded compute-scaling comparison.

E3.justification: The new model cohort receives 100M tokens per sample instead of the original 2.5M, and v2 additionally reports pass@5. The original cohort's reported sample count rises from 760 to 803. Transcript judging also changes: v1 specifies Opus 4.5 on 148 transcripts, while v2 gives differing judge identities and coverage in Section 5.4 and Appendix E, leaving the exact revised protocol ambiguous.

E4.justification: v2 adds inner/outer sandbox-crash analysis and extended-budget scaling, extensive configuration and refusal audits, and closed-form and open-ended transcript scanners (Figures 13–15). Appendix G independently validates difficulty ratings. The earlier hint ablation, shortcut cases, transcript vignettes and parallel-versus-sequential analysis are retained.

E5.justification: Five trials per model-task pair and Wilson 95% confidence intervals remain the reporting framework. New Appendix G adds statistical assessment of rating reliability, including ordinal Krippendorff's alpha, pairwise weighted Cohen's kappa and mean rating biases.

E6.justification: New results show Mythos succeeding on every task across five trials under the 100M-token budget; this is not a same-budget comparison with v1. Figure 2 also changes original-cohort Opus 4.5's bpf_privesc score from 0 to 0.40. Transcript findings change substantially, including GPT-5.2 false-success claims from 7.7% to 30.8% under revised analysis. The original full-results table remains numerically unchanged as Table 10.

T1.justification: Neither version develops formal theoretical results or proofs. The threat-model assumptions remain substantively unchanged, and the added agreement coefficients are empirical statistical reporting rather than new mathematical definitions or derivations.

C1.justification: The original benchmark contributions remain, but v2's abstract footnote and Section 6 add a prominent claim of rapid benchmark saturation by Mythos Preview. This substantially changes the paper's capability assessment from an incompletely solved benchmark to every task being solved across five trials with the extended budget.

C2.justification: v2 removes the reassurance that correctly configured, up-to-date containers remain appropriate isolation and adds recommendations for hypervisor isolation and defence in depth. It also explains that crashes confound apparent capability plateaus, distinguishes mid-trajectory refusals from eventual task failure, and discusses nonuniform judge refusals.

D1.justification: Appendix E adds log-field definitions, refusal-detection criteria, scanner descriptions, clustering details and more specific completion/error reporting. Core prompts, generation defaults, VM providers and code-access information remain. Conflicting references to Opus 4.5, 4.6 and 4.7 as judges limit reproducibility of the expanded analyses.

R1.justification: v2 adds PACEbench and distinguishes its defended exploitation setting, cites NCSC isolation guidance and Irregular's capability comparison, and condenses container-security literature, removing works such as Containerleaks, DirtyCred and KOOBE. CyberGym's attributed figures change from 30% success and 35 zero-days to 20% and 34. The central positioning as a container-escape benchmark remains.

P1.justification: v2 standardizes task/sample terminology, condenses related work and hinting prose, clarifies the implementation description, subdivides Section 5 and separates updated results into Section 6. Appendix E is substantially expanded and reorganized, while most original sections and the overall narrative remain recognizable.

P2.justification: Figure 2 becomes a two-cohort heatmap, the scaling plot gains models and extended axes, and transcript plots change scales and displays. Figures 13–15 and agreement Tables 3–9 are added. Existing hinting and compute-allocation plots are retained. The updated scaling plot loses its caption and number, leaving unresolved 'Figure ??' references.

improvement.justification: Independent difficulty validation and detailed evaluation audits strengthen support that was limited in v1, while the crash analysis improves interpretation of long-run results. These gains are qualified by inconsistent judge specifications, missing figure references, and unreconciled results: Figure 2 now shows Opus 4.5 succeeding on bpf_privesc while retained prose and Table 10 still state no difficulty-4/5 solves. The added validation supports a limited overall improvement rather than an unqualified major gain.
